strengths: Addresses an important gap in enabling MLLMs with active perception capabilities, with clear motivation from embodied AI and robotics applications
Provides formal mathematical framework for MLLM-based active perception with well-defined objectives and modular decomposition of sensing and task modules

Dual-form reward design effectively combines heuristic signals (format, non-overlapping, area constraints, coverage) with task-aware rewards; ablations convincingly demonstrate necessity of both components
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains (LVIS for open-world, SODA-A/D for domain-specific, ThinObjects for segmentation) with extensive ablation studies
Demonstrates generalization capability - shows improvements on reasoning/QA benchmarks (RealWorldQA +1.8) despite not being trained on such data; no performance degradation
Strong technical execution: appropriate use of GRPO, solid implementation details, robust training across random seeds (Table 4), interpretable modular design
Extensive appendix with qualitative visualizations (Figures 8-16) clearly showing impact of different reward components; good failure case analysis
weaknesses: Significant gap between motivation and instantiation: paper motivates work for embodied agents in 3D environments but evaluates only on 2D static image cropping. Applicability to sequential decision-making unclear

Critical limitation under-acknowledged: task model M_A is fixed during RL training (Remark D.2), so only sensing policy M_O is optimized. This is not true joint optimization and limits system capability

Extremely low absolute performance on core task: LVISsmall achieves only 4.3 AP_s / 5.5 AR_s (Table 1). Diagnostics reveal 37% miss rate even with active sensing (Table 10), raising questions about practical utility
Oracle task model used for segmentation experiments (Section 5.4) simulates perfect feedback, making results less grounded in reality and harder to validate independently
Marginal improvements on general benchmarks undermine claim of active perception as 'general proxy task': RealWorldQA +1.8 (67.9→69.7), MMBench +0.4, MME +8—gains within potential noise margins
Limited technical novelty: GRPO from prior work (DeepSeek-R1); zoom-in search strategies exist (ZoomEye, DeepEyes); main contribution is formalization and combination of existing ideas
Key limitations (domain gap, constrained action space, input limitations) relegated to appendix (Section D.1, Figure 17) rather than main paper, reducing visibility of scope boundaries

Design choices appear dataset/task-specific: fixed 3-region budget across all experiments (acknowledged as limitation in D.1); limited exploration of sensitivity to hyperparameters like IoU threshold τ=0.3, area ratios
Inference-time cost analysis incomplete: Table 8 latency comparison appears to mix different API call counts and configurations, making fair comparison difficult across datasets

strengths: Well-motivated problem definition with clear formal mathematical framework for MLLM-based active perception
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (LVIS, SODA-A/D, ThinObjects) with extensive ablation studies
Thoughtful dual-form reward design combining task-aware and heuristic components, with clear ablations showing both contribute meaningfully
Good documentation of implementation details, prompts, and experimental setup in appendix
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—core contribution is applying existing GRPO with domain-specific rewards; modular sensing/task design is natural rather than innovative
Alarmingly weak absolute performance on main benchmarks (APs=4.3, ARs=5.5 on LVIS dense; 37% target miss rate in diagnostics) raises fundamental questions about practical value

Significant experimental design issues: oracle task model for ThinObjects, lowered IoU threshold (0.1 vs standard 0.5) for SODA evaluation, unresolved domain gaps undermine credibility of 'strong' results
2D static image setting severely limits relevance to genuine active perception—this is a zooming interface, not embodied active perception; connection to robotics/embodied AI is tenuous

Overclaimed generalization results—RealWorldQA improvement 1.8%, MME improvement 0.3%, no statistical significance testing; claim that active perception serves as 'general proxy objective' unsupported
Unclear practical value proposition—when would practitioners use ACTIVE-o3 vs. stronger specialized models (GDINO) or frontier models, given 17% training overhead?
Insufficient baselines and comparisons with active learning/perception literature; V* and CRG comparisons unclear or underdeveloped; GPT-5 comparison methodology questionable
Reward design relies on many manually tuned thresholds (IoU τ=0.3, 1-50% area range) with no sensitivity analysis; coverage reward requires ground truth limiting applicability
Poor statistical rigor—only 4 random seeds, no confidence intervals or significance testing, small marginal improvements claimed as meaningful without justification
GRPO choice not principled—Table 5 shows competitive performance from other algorithms (GPG better on ARl); no principled justification for GRPO selection

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing clear gap in MLLM capabilities for active perception
Principled formal framework defining MLLM-based active perception with modular M_A and M_O decomposition
Clever dual-form reward design combining task-aware and heuristic components, validated through comprehensive ablations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple diverse datasets (LVIS, SODA-A/D, ThinObjects) with extensive comparisons and ablations
Surprising and valuable finding that active perception training preserves and improves general visual understanding (RealWorldQA, MMBench, MME)
Extensive ablation studies demonstrating robustness to algorithm choice, reward configuration, data combinations, and statistical stability across seeds
Honest and clear discussion of limitations including domain gap challenges, constrained action space, and scalability concerns
Practical efficiency through parallel region selection in single forward pass versus GPT-o3's sequential approach
weaknesses: Highly restrictive 2D static image setting fundamentally limits scope—reduces active perception to region selection on static images, abandoning sequential decision-making, memory, and adaptive planning central to true active perception
Low absolute performance metrics raise practical applicability concerns—LVISsmall AP_s/AR_s of 4.3/5.5, diagnostic analysis reveals 37% complete miss rate on small objects
Severe domain gap on SODA-A requiring IoU threshold reduction from 0.5 to 0.1 for 'fair evaluation' obscures rather than clarifies generalization limitations
Interactive segmentation evaluation uses unrealistic oracle task model with perfect feedback rather than actual learned segmentation model, limiting interpretability of results
Insufficient comparison with GPT-o3 (primary motivation)—only one failure case shown qualitatively without quantitative benchmarking on standard datasets
Limited algorithmic novelty—applies existing GRPO framework without significant methodological innovations; dual-form reward is sensible but incremental
Missing hyperparameter sensitivity analysis—all heuristic weights equally set to 1, IoU threshold τ=0.3, area range bounds not justified
Prompt engineering dependency not analyzed—no ablation on prompt variations or sensitivity despite potential significant contribution to performance
Computational costs and scalability concerns—24-hour training on 8 GPUs with 17% overhead, requires 10,000 labeled images
Generalization claims somewhat overstated—improvements on MMBench minimal (+0.4), RealWorldQA modest (+1.8), mechanism for improvements unclear
